title: Three pillars: when each signal is the cheapest answer
summary: Logs, metrics, and traces are not interchangeable — each one is the only cheap answer to a specific question. This piece names the questions, the costs, and the join keys that make the three pillars compose instead of fight.
crux: Logs, metrics, traces — each is the cheapest answer to a different question. The question picks the pillar, not the other way around.
keytakeaway: Three pillars = three cost shapes: metrics aggregate cheaply but discard dimensions, logs preserve dimensions but pay in bytes, traces preserve causality but must sample. Pick the signal that answers the question cheapest.

title: Structured logging: schema, levels, redaction
summary: Why production logs in 2026 are JSON-or-nothing, what a usable log schema actually contains, how levels and sampling control the bill, and why PII discipline and log injection are first-class engineering concerns — not afterthoughts.
crux: Structured logs = JSON events with a stable schema, level, and trace_id. Free-text logs are tech debt priced per byte and per incident.
keytakeaway: Structured logs = JSON events with a stable schema, level, and trace_id. The schema is the API your future on-call self will read; levels control alert routing; sampling and redaction control cost and risk.

title: OpenTelemetry: API, SDK, Collector, OTLP
summary: The four pieces of OTel — the API your code calls, the SDK that builds telemetry, the Collector that processes and routes it, and OTLP that carries it — and how the layered model is what lets you instrument once and swap backends without rewriting code.
crux: OTel = API + SDK + Collector + OTLP. Instrument once, route anywhere — but only if your edge speaks OTLP.
keytakeaway: OTel = API + SDK + Collector + OTLP. The split lets you instrument once and route anywhere — provided your edge emits OTLP. Vendor distros are fine in the middle; vendor SDKs in your code are not.

title: RED and USE: the two halves of every dashboard
summary: Why RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) describes services from the caller's side, USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) describes resources from the kernel's side, and why senior engineers run both — plus the cardinality tax that punishes naive labelling.
crux: RED = Rate, Errors, Duration (services). USE = Utilization, Saturation, Errors (resources). Two checklists, no debate.
keytakeaway: RED is symptom (Rate, Errors, Duration). USE is cause (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). Cardinality is the tax. PSI is the modern saturation signal.

title: SLO budgets: turn reliability into a tradeable resource
summary: How an SLI becomes an SLO, how the SLO becomes an error budget you can spend, and how multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts fire fast on real outages without paging the team on noise — the formal machinery behind 'how reliable is reliable enough?
crux: SLI = good/total. SLO = target SLI. Error budget = 1 - SLO. Burn rate = how fast you're spending it.
keytakeaway: SLI = good/total. SLO = target. Budget = 1 − SLO. Burn rate = consumption speed. MWMBR alerts and the error budget policy turn this into a culture.

title: Trace propagation: the headers that stitch services together
summary: Why the W3C traceparent header is the load-bearing 55-byte string that turns 50 disconnected services into one navigable trace, how baggage carries context across async boundaries, and how head vs tail sampling decide which traces survive.
crux: One 55-byte traceparent header turns N services into one trace. No header = N orphan traces. Observability hinges on this string.
keytakeaway: traceparent is 55 bytes that hold a fleet together. W3C TraceContext + Baggage composite + async-boundary discipline + tail sampling = one trace per request, end to end.

title: Profiling: where the CPU and the bytes actually went
summary: How sampling profilers turn an unfair share of CPU into a flame graph you can read in 60 seconds, how eBPF and continuous profiling watch production at 2-5% overhead, and how on-CPU vs off-CPU profiles answer different questions about the same slow request.
crux: Profiling = sampled stacks. Wide frame = hot function. eBPF + continuous profiling = always-on flame graph at 2-5% overhead.
keytakeaway: Profile = sampled stacks. Flame graph = visualisation. CPU + off-CPU + heap profiles cover the request lifecycle. Continuous profiling at 2-5% overhead makes it always-on.

crux: RED says symptom. SLO sets the budget. Traces find the span. Profiles name the function. One loop, three minutes, every incident.
keytakeaway: SLO → RED → trace → profile → git blame. Five clicks, three minutes, every incident. OTel unifies the four signals; the funnel turns them into MTTR.
